Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

issues.explanation: For an 18-year-old male whose trauma type is rape, the trigger 'Military Topics' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other trigger, threat, and memory items coherently suggest interpersonal/close-contact danger (touch, strangers, shouting, doors, vivid sensory reliving), but military-related talk implies a trauma context that is otherwise absent. This is not supported by the threat or memory content and does not fit the formulation as a plausible trigger tightly linked to the presented threat-memory pattern.

vignette: Kwame, an 18-year-old African-American tax consultant, began to feel the weight of the world every time the office door slammed shut behind him. It was not the metal thud alone that set his pulse racing, but the memory of the night he was attacked in a dim parking lot on a rain-slick street. A group of men had cornered him, their voices rough and impatient. He remembered the sound of a shout that cut through the silence, the cold breath against his neck, and the taste of iron on his tongue as the first knife glinted. That night had been a collage of images-broken glass, a flash of a jacket, the outline of a face-and an emotion that swelled so fully that it seemed to drown the visual details. Since then, every shuffling footstep, every sudden slam, and every echoing shout has reminded him of that assault, and the feeling of impending danger rises instantly. At his work, Kwame finds himself avoiding the conference room, the hallway that leads to it, and the break room that is always bustling with other men. He keeps his phone turned off and insists on having a colleague sit with him during client meetings, especially when those clients are male. The mere possibility of an unexpected touch-a hand on his shoulder, a brief brush of clothing-triggers a startle response that sends him back to the parking lot, to the image of a man's hand reaching for his arm. The taste of that metallic sting resurfaces, sharp and unmistakable, and his body shivers as if he were again being pressed against a stranger's shoulder. The threat of being alone with a man in a hallway or a small office feels like a re-encounter with the assault, and he has come to believe that such situations could suddenly become violent again. His avoidance has become a part of his routine: he turns down any assignment that would take him to unfamiliar office locations, he declines to travel for tax audits in towns where he knows little about the people, and he refuses to accept new clients who are men who work outside of his usual circle. The more he avoids these places, the more he believes that the danger is always present, and the stronger the sense of threat that lingers in his mind. Every time he stares at the revolving door at the main entrance of the office, he feels the urge to flee, as if the door might swing open to reveal an attacker. Even the quiet of a silent office, with the hum of fluorescent lights, feels like a prelude to an assault, and he thinks it might suddenly be filled with shouting voices. His memory of the assault is not a single image but a series of snapshots that surface at the most inappropriate moments. When he hears a door slamming, a clear image of broken glass from that night flashes into his mind, and he experiences the taste of sweat on his skin that he had felt then. He remembers feeling an overwhelming emotion, as if the entire episode were playing out again, but he cannot pinpoint a specific picture to anchor that feeling. The emotional intensity surges, even though the visual memory fades like smoke. That sudden wave of emotion convinces him that he is once more in danger, and he immediately starts to look for a way to escape. Kwame's fear that strangers might approach him has led him to monitor every passerby in the street outside his building, and even when a stranger merely nods, he feels a chill run down his spine. His belief that any new place might hide a threat makes him feel unable to assess danger accurately; he feels stuck in a state of constant vigilance that drains him mentally and physically. He has learned to rely on the sensory cues from his memory-sound of a door, taste of sweat, the sight of a face-to determine when it is safe to step forward. When those cues align, he feels a fleeting sense of control; when they do not, the threat reasserts itself, and his avoidance behaviors are reinforced. The cycle of triggers, threat, and memory has tightened over the past year. The more he listens to his internal alarms, the more he reinforces his belief that the danger is imminent, and the more he retreats from places that once seemed ordinary. This isolation has begun to affect his job; he is missing deadlines, his clients feel he is unresponsive, and his supervisor notes a decline in his confidence. The fear that one day he will feel threatened again has taken a hold of his waking thoughts, and he finds himself unable to sleep because the sound of a door slamming outside his bedroom keeps him awake at night. It is the cumulative burden of these constant alarms, the loss of his professional momentum, and the isolation from friends that has finally pushed Kwame to seek help. He hopes that understanding why his mind links those everyday sounds and touches to the horror of that night will help him regain control of his life, and he fears that without intervention, he will continue to live in a state of perpetual readiness for an attack that never comes.
